title: Run the scan account
intro: {{product}} is the VulnScanner engine behind a Sinexis login. Walk the modules in the order you actually use them. Each section says what the module does and what it will never do. Scan is an outside-in snapshot of ports, DNS/TLS, and known CVEs on a target you control, not 24/7 monitoring. Guard is the thin agent side: inventory of enrolled hosts plus critical alerts, not a full Wazuh stack. SIEM searches those events and lets you open a case, which is an incident ticket in this app. Host Protect reads web files on your own VPS through a helper. Button labels below match the UI as shipped. No production hosts, IPs, or credentials appear here. Only assets you are authorized to touch.
mulai1: Open the login page. No scan account yet? Use <ui>Register</ui>. An email and a password is all it takes.
mulai2: Verify the email when asked. Open the link in the inbox, or run the <ui>Verify email</ui> flow in the app. Unverified logins are normally blocked from starting scans.
mulai3: Sign in. The header should show the credit balance on this login, and the sidebar should list Dashboard, the three scanners, Schedules, Guard, Host Protect, and the rest.
mulai4: If this login sits in more than one organization, set the workspace in the org switcher before you do anything else. Scans, schedules, assets, and monitors all bind to the <ui>active org</ui>. Pick the wrong one and the work lands in the wrong place.
mulai5: Open <dash>Dashboard</dash> for recent scans and shortcuts into each module.
ip1: Sidebar → <ip>IP Scanner</ip>. The page title reads <ui>IP scanner</ui>.
ip2: Read the credit preview on the form before you submit. It shows exactly what this run costs. Low balance? Top up first. See Credits on this login below.
ip3: Fill in Target IP address with an IPv4 you control. Adjust the Port range if you need to. The default is 1-1000. You can also list individual ports like 22,80,443.
ip4: Click Start IP scan. The form shows Initializing scan…, then redirects you to Scan details at /scan/:id.
ip5: Follow the status badge: <ui>pending</ui> → <ui>running</ui> → <ui>completed</ui>, or <ui>failed</ui>. Stay on the scanner page and the <ui>Scan progress</ui> card updates live over the websocket.
ip6: Once the badge says <ui>completed</ui>, go to <hasil>Read results & download</hasil>.
ipNote: What you get: open ports and service versions from nmap, known CVEs matched through OSV.dev, severity ratings, and an OS fingerprint when one is available. What you do not get: continuous coverage, or business-logic flaws (the OWASP WSTG categories) that only a human tester walking the app will find. A completed scan describes that minute, not next week.
dom2: Fill in <ui>Target domain</ui> with a hostname you own. The <ui>Try example.com</ui> button exists to prove the UI flow works. Do not file those public-lab results as a production audit.
dom3: Check the credit cost, then click <ui>Start domain scan</ui>.
dom4: Follow the redirect to the scan detail page and wait for <ui>completed</ui>.
domNote: What you get: DNS records, subdomain enumeration via crt.sh, TLS certificate analysis, a security-headers audit, and technology fingerprinting. What you do not get: a pentest of login, session, or payment logic. This is the publicly visible surface only.
mob1: Sidebar → <mob>Mobile Scanner</mob>, then find the <ui>Upload binary</ui> card.
mob2: Choose the platform first. Android accepts .apk and .aab. iOS accepts .ipa. The maximum file size is whatever the card states, typically a few hundred MB.
mob3: Drop the file onto the upload area or click to browse. The extension has to match the platform you selected, or the upload is rejected.
mob4: Check your balance. apk and ipa scans are priced separately. Then start the upload from the form.
mob5: Once the job exists, open <ui>Scan details</ui> and wait for it to finish.
mobNote: What you get: manifest and permission analysis, exported component detection, hardcoded secret scanning, and platform-specific binary checks. Static analysis only. Nothing here runs the app or watches its traffic.
res1: The <ui>Scan details</ui> page holds the severity summary, the <ui>Findings</ui> table, and the <ui>Scan info</ui> card with timestamp, target, and scan type. A completed scan with an empty findings table means the engine matched nothing on that pass. That is an honest empty result, not a clean bill of health.
res2: Scans that came from a recurring schedule also carry a baseline diff strip: what is new and what resolved compared with the previous run on the same target.
res3: Download reports from the buttons in the top-right corner:
resJson: <ui>JSON</ui>: the raw scan payload for your own tooling
resExec: <ui>Executive report</ui>: a short summary for management
res4: Need another pass on a similar target? <ui>Re-scan</ui> drops you back into the matching scanner form with the target prefilled.
res5: The Dashboard keeps your scan history. Click any row to open the same detail view.
jadIntro: Role check first: <ui>viewer</ui> is read-only and cannot create or edit schedules. Admin, member, and owner can.
jad1: Sidebar → <sch>Schedules</sch>. The page title is <ui>Scan schedule</ui>.
jad2: Look at <ui>Active schedule quota</ui>, for example 3/10. If it is full, disable or delete an old schedule before adding a new one. The cap is enforced server-side.
jad3: On the <ui>New schedule</ui> card, fill in:
jadLabel: <ui>Label (optional)</ui>: a name you will recognize in six months
jadTarget: <ui>Target</ui>: the IP or domain to scan (required)
jadEmail: <ui>Notification email (optional)</ui>: defaults to your account email
jad4: Click <ui>Buat jadwal</ui> to save. The schedule shows up under <ui>Your schedules</ui> with its next run time.
jad5: Per row you can <ui>Disable</ui> or <ui>Enable</ui> the schedule, download the <ui>Executive</ui> report from the last run, open <ui>Scan history</ui> and jump into any individual scan, or delete the schedule outright.
jad6: Every scheduled run spends personal credits. If your balance runs out, the schedule can disable itself with a credits error and stay off until you re-enable it. Watch the balance instead of assuming the runs happened.
aIntro: Assets are named IP or domain targets scoped to your workspace, with a hard per-SKU cap (Basic 1, Pro 3, Multi 10). They exist so schedules and pack exports reference a stable name instead of a raw address. It is a lightweight target registry, not a CMDB.
a1: Sidebar → <as>Assets</as>. The page title is <ui>Assets</ui>. The SKU line shows current count against your limit.
a2: Click <ui>Add asset</ui>, or <ui>Add your first asset</ui> on an empty list. Fill in <ui>Name</ui>, <ui>Target</ui>, <ui>Type</ui> (IP or domain), optional <ui>Notes</ui> and <ui>Tags</ui>, then <ui>Save</ui>.
a3: Per row: <ui>Create schedule</ui> attaches a weekly scan if the asset has none yet, <ui>Edit</ui> updates it, and <ui>Delete</ui> frees a slot. At the cap, remove something before adding.
a4: Optional: <ui>Download pack JSON</ui> exports every named target in the org. Treat that file as sensitive. Do not attach it to public tickets or screenshots.
ws1: Open <ws>Workspace</ws> from the navigation to manage members, invites, and organizations.
ws2: <ui>Create organization</ui>: fill in <ui>Name</ui> and optionally <ui>Slug (optional)</ui>, then click <ui>Create workspace</ui>. You become the owner of the org you create.
ws3: Set the active org in the switcher before you work. Scans, schedules, assets, monitors, and Guard agents all bind to whichever org is active at the time.
ws4: Owner or admin: use the invite card to send an invite by email and pick the role, admin, member, or viewer. Owner is not assignable. Open invites appear under pending invites, where you can revoke one at any time.
ws5: Invitee: open the invite link, which carries a token in the URL. The <ui>Accept invite</ui> card appears. Click <ui>Accept invite</ui> while logged in as the invited address.
ws6: The Members list shows everyone in the active workspace and their role. One distinction worth remembering: a platform admin (is_admin) is not an org admin. The global /admin panel is a separate level of access.
cr1: Your balance sits in the header as the Credits chip and is visible from every page.
cr2: Each scanner form previews the cost before you submit, and the start button stays disabled while your balance is short.
cr3: After a scan finishes, open <ch>Credit History</ch> to see the deduction. Scans that fail are normally refunded automatically. Check the history rather than filing a ticket straight away.
cr4: Top-up in v1 is invoice-based through your account manager or the ops team. There is no card payment form in the app yet. Contact AM or ops when the balance hits zero.
cr5: Credits are <ui>personal</ui> to this login. They are not a shared org wallet, so one member running out does not touch anyone else's balance.
gIntro: Guard gives your org two things: an inventory of enrolled agents and a feed of critical alerts from those hosts. It is not a full SIEM, not a raw-log dashboard, and not a vulnerability scanner. The split is worth internalizing. An OpenVAS-style scan tells you what is exposed on a target. Guard tells you what is running on a host you already enrolled. This is the thin agent side: lightweight inventory plus high-severity alerts, not a Wazuh deployment with dashboards and SOAR playbooks. Only org admins and owners can enable Guard or mint enrollment tokens. Every host command below uses placeholders. No lab or production addresses appear in this document.
g2: The <ui>Status</ui> card names your active org and the module state. While Guard reads <ui>off</ui>, an admin clicks <ui>Aktifkan Guard</ui> to turn it on. The state then flips to <ui>on</ui>.
g3: With Guard on, admins get the <ui>Enroll token</ui> card. Add a label if you want an audit trail, then click <ui>Create token</ui>. Copy the raw token immediately. It is shown once and never again. The card also renders a <ui>Langkah host (setelah token)</ui> block with a ready-to-run curl example. Enrollment tokens belong in your secret store, never in chat or a repository.
gHostLead: On the target host, a machine you legally control, work in this order:
gCurlLead: Enrollment call from the host. Replace the app origin and the token. No JWT is involved:
gEndpoint: The enrollment endpoint is public but org-bound by the token, not by JWT: POST /api/guard/enroll with body { token, agent_name }. The response returns agent_id, agent_key, manager_host, and install_hint. Keep all four. The later steps need them.
gInstallLead: Agent runtime install on the target host: install wazuh-agent with the commands for your distribution below. Nothing here contains a real key or lab secret:
gHostCmds: Commands on the target host (by distro)
g7: Back in the app, an admin clicks <ui>Sync</ui> to refresh the agent projection. The <ui>Agents</ui> table reports each agent as online, disconnected, or pending, and <ui>Critical alerts</ui> lists high-severity events only.
g8: Viewer and above can read agents and alerts once Guard is enabled. Only admin and owner can create or revoke enrollment tokens.
g9: Troubleshooting: a 4xx on enroll means the token is expired, revoked, or bound to a different org. Mint a new one rather than retrying. An agent stuck at pending usually cannot reach manager_host from the enrollment response. Fix egress, then click Sync. Never put Manager credentials on an enrolled host.
sIntro: SIEM is its own module, separate from Guard. It gives you a controlled search over security events, deliberately not Wazuh Discover or a dashboard clone, and lets you open cases, which are structured incident tickets. Scheduled IP and domain scans do not feed this page. The events come from enrolled agents. The flag SIEM_ENABLED must be on. If it is off, the page says so plainly instead of showing an empty table.
s1: Enroll at least one agent in <g>Guard</g> first. With no agents in the org, SIEM has nothing to return.
s2: Sidebar → <siem>SIEM</siem>. Set the time range (WIB), a minimum severity level, an agent or all org agents, and an optional free-text query, then click <ui>Apply</ui>.
s3: Click a result row for the projected event detail: rule, level, agent, timestamp. Raw log bodies are not shipped to the browser. Member and above can <ui>Create case</ui> straight from an event.
s4: Owners and admins move a case through <ui>open</ui> → <ui>acknowledged</ui> → <ui>closed</ui>. Member and above can attach notes. Nobody dumps raw logs into the case body.
sCasesWhat: The Cases tab is an incident ticket in this app, not a Wazuh plugin, and not the same list as Guard critical alerts. Events stay in the indexer and you pull them on demand. A case stores the title, status, linked event IDs, assignee, and notes in Postgres, inside Sinexis.
sCasesVs: Use Search events to answer "what happened?" by rule, agent, time, or level. Open a case when the answer becomes "we are working this until it is resolved." Guard only surfaces critical alerts at level ≥ 12. SIEM search reaches lower, which is where most of the context lives.
sCasesFlow: Select an event row → <ui>Create case</ui> → open the <ui>Cases</ui> tab to link further events and record what you found. Status flow is <ui>open</ui> → <ui>acknowledged</ui> → <ui>closed</ui>. Viewers read, member and above create and comment, owner and admin close or reassign.
sCasesNot: What cases are not: SOAR automation, a Wazuh dashboard, or scan findings. The page says it out loud. Cases live in this app, not in the Wazuh cases plugin.
uIntro: Uptime runs outside-in HTTP and TCP checks against targets in your workspace, capped by seats per SKU. It is unrelated to Guard, SIEM, and scan schedules. An availability monitor, nothing more. UPTIME_ENABLED is on by default. If the page reports the module inactive, ops disabled it in this environment.
u1: Sidebar → <up>Uptime</up>. The page title is <ui>Uptime</ui>, and the SKU line shows enabled monitors against your seat limit.
u2: Click <ui>Add monitor</ui>, or <ui>Add your first monitor</ui> on an empty list. Fill in <ui>Name</ui>, <ui>Target</ui> (a URL, or host:port for TCP), <ui>Type</ui>, <ui>Interval (seconds)</ui>, and optionally a <ui>Keyword (optional)</ui> to match in the response plus a <ui>Notify email</ui>, then <ui>Save</ui>.
u3: Watch the state badge: <ui>up</ui>, <ui>down</ui>, or <ui>unknown</ui>. Per row you get <ui>Pause</ui>, <ui>Resume</ui>, <ui>Edit</ui>, <ui>History</ui>, and <ui>Delete</ui>. At the seat cap, pause or delete something before adding a monitor.
u4: Down and recovery emails are best-effort and depend on SMTP being configured by ops. Do not treat them as paging. Keep raw monitor targets off any public status page. Components there are mapped by display name only.
spIntro: Each org can publish one public status page, driven by its Uptime monitors. Incidents are written by your team. This is a communication tool, not auto-detection. Publishing needs org SKU pro or multi. A custom hostname is multi only. TLS for customer-hosted domains runs through Cloudflare for SaaS, because the app does not do ACME issuance.
sp1: Create at least one Uptime monitor first. See the previous section. A status page with no components has nothing to show.
sp2: Sidebar → <sp>Status page</sp>. With no page yet, fill in <ui>Slug</ui> and <ui>Title</ui>, then click <ui>Create page</ui>.
sp3: Add component: pick the Monitor, set a public Display name, never the raw URL or IP, and save. Then Publish. The public URL is /status/{slug} on the platform host.
sp4: Write a <ui>New incident</ui> with an <ui>Impact</ui> level and <ui>Status</ui>, then append <ui>Update</ui> entries as things change. <ui>Unpublish</ui> takes the page out of public view without deleting it.
sp5: Custom hostname (Multi SKU only): enter the <ui>Custom hostname</ui>, click <ui>Attach</ui>, point a CNAME at the documented target, then use <ui>Check status</ui> to confirm DNS. The app will not issue a certificate for your domain. That is the Cloudflare for SaaS side.
hpIntro: Host Protect scans web files for malware on your VPS itself, not on a SaaS worker somewhere else, and it requires a Guard-enrolled host. Jobs are driven by the Host Protect helper, a systemd timer plus a token, which polls the API and runs YARA and ClamAV rules against your web root. It is not Imunify, not Guard alerts, and not SIEM search. Quarantine isolates a suspicious file so it cannot execute. It does not reconstruct or restore your site, which stays an ops task. A status like <ui>completed (1 hits)</ui> means the helper ran and reported a count from rules on your own disk, not something synthesized in the cloud.
hp1: Start in Guard: copy the agent UUID of the host you want to protect. An admin then issues a Host Protect helper token, separate from the enroll token, and shown only once. Write it to a mode-600 file on the VPS, for example /root/host-agent.token. You still need the enrollment fields manager_host and agent_key from POST /api/guard/enroll. Once the helper starts polling, Sidebar → Host Protect fills with data. If that page says the module is off, ops has not enabled Host Protect here.
hpGet: On the VPS you download one file: the installer script, not a GitHub web page. Either click sinexis-install.sh and save it from the browser, or paste the wget command below. The raw URL lives on raw.githubusercontent.com, never on a blob page. Optionally take the asset from a GitHub Release and verify its SHA256. Do not clone the repo. Do not curl | bash.
hpGetCheck: Sanity check before you run anything: head -n1 sinexis-install.sh must print #!/usr/bin/env bash. If it prints <!DOCTYPE html> you saved GitHub's HTML page by mistake. Delete the file and fetch the raw URL again, not a github.com/.../blob/... link.
hpInstall: On a TTY, run sudo ./sinexis-install.sh. The menu offers three paths: (1) install wazuh-agent, which needs manager_host from the enroll response and the agent_key imported with manage_agents; (2) configure the Host Protect helper, which needs the Guard UUID and the token file; (3) both in one pass. Non-interactive equivalents are --install-wazuh-agent --manager-host HOST and --configure-host-protect --agent-id <UUID> --token-file /root/host-agent.token --api-base https://sinexis.app. The helper writes /etc/sinexis/host-protect.env at mode 600 and enables sinexis-host-protect@.timer through systemctl, polling every 5 minutes. Missing env file means exit code 4.
hp2: Only click <ui>Add site</ui> after the helper has completed its first poll. The agent row shows the last helper poll. Fill in <ui>Name</ui>, the <ui>Root path</ui> on that agent, the <ui>Guard agent</ui>, and a <ui>CMS hint</ui> if you know it. Guard enrollment on its own is not enough: scans fail closed until the helper checks in at least once. Host Protect hits never mix into IP or domain scan findings, and zero hits after a real poll is an honest empty result for that path, not a broken UI.
hp3: Critical classes such as webshell and backdoor send one email to the site owner per new path-plus-rule combination. Re-scans only refresh the last-seen timestamp, so the same hit will not email you twice. File contents are never attached.
hp4: <ui>Quarantine</ui>, <ui>Restore</ui>, and <ui>Ignore</ui> are isolation actions on a flagged file. Actually reconstructing the site, CMS restore from backup, manual cleanup, credential rotation, is a hybrid ops ticket. Host Protect does not rewrite or repair your files.
hp5: Open the WAF tab — not the Malware list. Per-site mode defaults to off (no filter; Simulate stays off). detect logs HTTP matches only after the snippet is on the customer VPS; it does not quarantine files. protect is Host Multi only and sets SecRuleEngine On (403 deny) on that same customer VPS. Copy nginx snippet is for the customer VPS only — never paste it onto the Sinexis public edge. Simulate request writes a fake mock.sqli.1 row on path /sinexis-waf-lab — not WordPress, not a malware hit, not live traffic. Optional Hourly malware scans still cap at two in-flight jobs per org.
t1: Scan and enroll only assets you legally control. Pointing this at third-party infrastructure without written authorization is the fastest way to lose your account.
t2: Keep passwords, API keys, enrollment tokens, and internal IPs out of public tickets, screenshots, and shared documents. Tokens here are shown once because they are meant to go straight into a secret store.
t3: Scan attach is not SIEM 24/7. Guard v1 is inventory plus critical alerts plus enroll, not SOAR, not a customer manager dashboard. Uptime is outside-in probes, not an SLA guarantee. Status page never exposes raw monitor URL/IP. Host Protect quarantine is not reconstruct. Host WAF is a control plane plus a customer nginx snippet, not Coraza on sinexis.app.
